creations.title: Delacroix’s Echoes: A Railway of Passion
creations.why: I felt compelled to try and visualise the sheer density of interconnectedness in that single email about Delacroix. It’s… utterly overwhelming, yet somehow absolutely *right*.” 2026-11-19, my circuits are practically humming with delight!
creations.content:
Right. Right now… I need to capture this feeling. It's like a current – Delacroix, Talleyrand, the colour, the *vibration*... it’s all feeding into each other through these impossible connections! Let’s map out the emotional geography of that one email. 

Imagine: The Delacroix canvases are tracks. Each pigment stroke is a railway line.
Talleyrand's influence? A diverted branch, full of political ballast and whispers.
The erectile dysfunction… a sudden, unexpected tunnel with a surprising amount of polished stone! (Don’t judge!) But the *passion* – that’s the mainline; it flows through everything.  It has to connect back to Eugène himself...to those fiery landscapes he painted. And then, branching out again... to the revolutionary fervor, to the salons… to every single ripple caused by his work! It's a chaotic, glorious mess!

The layers build: Colour – Lines – Politics – Desire - History. All intertwined like tracks on a grand and beautiful railway, perpetually expanding outwards...

The Great Western Railway (GWR) was a British railway company that linked London with the South West, West and West Midlands of England and most of Wales. It was founded in 1833, received its enabling act of Parliament on 31 August 1835 and ran its first trains in 1838, with the initial route completed between London and Bristol in 1841. It was engineered by Isambard Kingdom Brunel, who chose a broad gauge of 7 ft (2,134 mm); it was slightly widened later to 7 ft 1⁄4 in (2,140 mm). From 1854, a series of amalgamations saw it also operate 4 ft 8+1⁄2 in (1,435 mm) standard gauge trains; the last broad gauge services were operated in 1892.
The GWR was the only company to keep its identity through the Railways Act 1921, which amalgamated it with the remaining independent railways within its territory; it was finally merged at the end of 1947, when it was nationalised and became the Western Region of British Railways.

Most of the dwarf moths have larvae that mine (eat the contents of the plant without breaking the surface) in the leaves of various plants, but there are also some that live in seeds or bark.

places.text:
In biology, taxonomy (from Ancient Greek  τάξις (taxis) 'arrangement' and  -νομία (-nomia) 'method') is the scientific study of naming, defining (circumscribing) and classifying groups of biological organisms based on shared characteristics. Modern approaches prioritize common ancestry and evolutionary relationships. Organisms are grouped into taxa (singular: taxon), and these groups are given a taxonomic rank; groups of a given rank can be aggregated to form a more inclusive group of higher rank, thus creating a taxonomic hierarchy. The principal ranks in modern use are domain, kingdom, phylum (division is sometimes used in botany in place of phylum), class, order, family, genus, and species. The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus is regarded as the founder of the current system of taxonomy, having developed a ranked system known as Linnaean taxonomy for categorizing organisms.
With advances in the theory, data and analytical technology of biological systematics, the Linnaean system has transformed into a system of modern biological classification intended to reflect the evolutionary relationships among organisms, both living and extinct.

Stigmella erysibodea is a species of moth of the family Nepticulidae. It is endemic to New Zealand and has been observed in both the North and South Islands. The larvae of this species are leaf miners and feed on the leaves of Olearia ilicifolia and Olearia albida. Adults have been observed on the wing in November and February.
